question: How did the CIDOC CRM SIG revise the scope note for the property covering type/classification assignment (Issue 97), and why was the requirement that the classifying act be 'scientific' dropped?
gold_answer: Martin Doerr's original wording restricted the class to entities that are 'scientifically' classified. Tony Gill objected that this would wrongly exclude everyday cataloguing acts such as assigning Dewey classmarks, subject headings, or iconographic classifications, which are squarely within the CRM's intended scope. Martin agreed, and the accepted revision dropped 'scientifically', instead describing the act simply as classifying an entity (an object, specimen, action, or concept), where the value of the classification depends on the identity of the classifier and the date it was made; the note kept its reference to biological 'determination' (systematic/molecular identification of a specimen) as a covered case.
key_facts: The original scope note required the classifying act to be done 'scientifically'
Tony Gill argued this would exclude ordinary classification acts like Dewey classmarks, subject headings, and iconographic classifications
Martin Doerr agreed and the word 'scientifically' was removed from the accepted wording
The revised note explicitly retained biological 'determination' (systematic/molecular identification of a specimen) as an example within scope
produced_answer: Issue 97 concerned E17 Type Assignment (subclass of Attribute Assignment). Martin Doerr's original proposed scope note (2002-10-09) read: 'This entity describes the act of scientifically classifying some entity, an object, a work, an action or whatever. The value of classification depends critically on general and personal knowledge and the scientific system used... This entity comprises also the process of "determination", i.e. the systematic and molecular identification of a specimen in biology.' Tony Gill (2002-10-15) recommended dropping the word 'scientifically' because it could be read to exclude assignments such as Dewey classmarks, subject headings, and iconographic classifications, which were meant to be well within the CRM's practical and intended scope. He proposed rewording to: 'This entity describes the act of classifying another entity, for example an object, a specimen, an action or a concept. The value of classification depends critically on the identity of the classifier and the date that the classification was assigned. This entity also comprises the process of "determination"...' Martin agreed the same day ('I agree'). Edmund Lee then raised a follow-up question about whether 'indexing' should also be mentioned or is covered by the superclass. The word 'scientific/scientifically' does not appear in the current (v7.1.3) E17 scope note retrieved via `search.py concept E17`, confirming the change was adopted.

question: How did the CIDOC CRM SIG's notion of 'CRM compatibility' evolve during 2008, and what did the resulting draft definition specify?
gold_answer: In April 2008 Martin Doerr raised the issue because claims of CRM compatibility were increasing with no agreed criteria behind them; the ensuing discussion among Nicholas Crofts, Stephen Stead, Edmund Lee and Guenther Goerz surfaced sharp disagreement over whether compatibility should rest on independently verifiable tests, tiered levels of conformance, or certification by a trusted authority (plus a proposed compatibility logo), and concluded that none of this existed yet. By September 2008, acting on decisions taken at the May CRM-SIG meeting, Martin circulated a formal draft text, intended as an amendment to ISO 21127, defining compatibility as preserving data 'without loss of meaning with respect to the CRM concepts', distinguishing import/export compatibility from integrated-access compatibility, and letting communities restrict compatibility to an explicitly declared CRM subset. After Vladimir Ivanov pressed on how meaning-preservation could be judged, Martin added a concrete counterexample of an incompatible structure ('Physical Object has date: Time-Span' — importable into CRM form but not losslessly exportable back), while the mechanism for verifying or certifying such claims was still unresolved and left for further discussion.
key_facts: Martin's April 2008 posting was prompted by rising compatibility claims with no agreed criteria; proposals discussed included independently verifiable tests, a certifying authority, tiered conformance levels, and a compatibility logo
By September 2008 Martin circulated a draft definition, based on decisions from the May CRM-SIG meeting, intended as an ISO 21127 amendment
The draft defined compatibility as no 'loss of meaning with respect to the CRM concepts' and allowed communities to restrict compatibility to an explicit CRM subset
Following Vladimir Ivanov's feedback, Martin added a counterexample of an incompatible structure: 'Physical Object has date: Time-Span', which can be imported but not losslessly exported
produced_answer: The notion evolved through several stages across 2008. April 21-28 (t0383): Martin Doerr opened the issue noting 'increasing claims of compatibility with the CIDOC CRM' and proposed a minimal working definition (ability to represent certain kinds of possibly multiple events associated with a Thing or Actor), which triggered a broad debate: Edmund Lee distinguished system compliance from dataset compliance; Nicholas Crofts laid out two compliance paradigms (independently verifiable criteria vs. certification authority), proposed graded conformance levels and a compatibility logo; Stephen Stead framed compatibility as 'no semantic loss' through data transforms and proposed concrete interoperability test questions; Guenther Goerz challenged whether strict compatibility can even be decided given the CRM's natural-language scope notes; Nick Poole (Collections Trust) offered to help build certification infrastructure. May 28 (t0392): after the May CRM-SIG meeting, Martin circulated 'an analysis of the requirement' distilled from the email debate, with a tentative plan to have a normative draft ready before the CIDOC 2008 conference for plenary approval. September 2-13 (t0400): Martin circulated a full draft text fleshing out the May decisions, introducing the core criterion of encoding 'without loss of meaning with respect to the CRM concepts' -- judged by an expert conversant in both source and CRM, not by an automatic test -- and allowing communities to restrict compatibility to an explicitly declared subset of CRM concepts. Vladimir Ivanov pushed on intensional/extensional meaning and asked for a counterexample of incompatibility; Martin supplied one ('Physical Object has date: Time-Span' as import/export-incompatible). October 7 (t0407): Martin sent a formal 'Call for Comment' on 'Definition of compatibility with ISO21127' (document V4, tied to CRM v4.2.6), meant to replace the old 'Compatibility with the CRM' section and to give high-level objectives/criteria (not a full logical definition), plus a minimal OWL 'reduced CRM-compatible form,' for discussion at the Nov 6-7 London SIG meeting. November 3 (t0417): Bernhard Schiemann sent a detailed section-by-section critique of V4; Martin's point-by-point replies pinned down the definition: a 'CRM-compatible form' is any encoding of CRM instances in a formal language that preserves the relations between CRM classes, properties and inheritance rules (explicitly excluding cardinality restrictions, which would violate the CRM's intended monotonic schema); a 'reduced CRM-compatible form' is a declared subset such that every instance of the reduced form is also a valid instance of the full CRM-compatible form; the draft distinguished import-compatible, export-compatible (and partial versions of each), and access-compatible (integrated-access) systems, with 'semantic reduction to CRM concepts' as the export mechanism. November 4-6 (t0420): a side vote settled the wording of the verification/certification clause, with members (Marco Neumann, Christian-Emil Ore, Bernhard Schiemann) debating options and converging on an alternative requiring providers to publish verification procedures or obtain third-party certification. November 14-16 (t0427): following the London meeting, Martin circulated CIDOC CRM v4.3 containing the adopted compatibility chapter, with a final vote on the closing certification phrase: 'The provider should be able to demonstrate the claim with suitable test data... The provider should either make evidence of these procedures publicly available on the Internet on a site nominated by the ISO community of use, so that any third party is able to verify the claim with suitable test data, or acquire a certificate by a certification authority (CA)... The CA will grant the provider of the certified system the right to use the "CRM compatible" logo.' Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore approved; this became part of CRM version 5.0, to be submitted to ISO as a proposed amendment to ISO 21127.

question: When someone wanted to model the relationship between a manuscript's digital facsimile, its normalized transcription, and the original manuscript, what property did the SIG recommend for linking the transcription back to what it was derived from, and how did that recommendation relate to the alternative FRBRoo property that was also suggested?
gold_answer: Dieter Köhler asked how to express that a transcription is not identical to, but derived from, a facsimile/scan of a manuscript, since neither 'refers to' nor 'represents' captured the relationship. Joao Oliveira suggested the FRBRoo property 'is derivative of' (R58), but Martin Doerr recommended the CRM's own property 'shows features of' (P130, with a P130.1 kind-of-similarity value such as 'Transcript'), and clarified that P130 is a generalization of R58, so both proposals were correct at their respective levels (CRM versus FRBRoo). Köhler then pushed back that R58 implies a substantial content modification, which felt too strong for a faithful transcription, and suggested 'is realised in' (R65) might fit better — a question the thread left as depending on how much the transcription changes or standardizes its source, without a single rule settling it for every case.
key_facts: Dieter Köhler's problem was linking a transcription to the manuscript/facsimile it derives from, since neither P67 'refers to' nor P138 'represents' fit
Joao Oliveira proposed the FRBRoo property R58 'is derivative of'
Martin Doerr recommended CRM's P130 'shows features of' (with P130.1 kind of similarity, e.g. 'Transcript') and stated P130 is a generalization of R58, making both correct

Koehler argued R58 implies substantial content modification and suggested R65 'is realised in' might suit a faithful transcription better, leaving the exact choice dependent on how much the transcription alters its source
produced_answer: In the January 2008 thread 'Relations between information objects', Dieter Köhler asked how to link a normalized transcription back to the manuscript/facsimile it was derived from, since neither P67 refers to nor P138 represents seemed accurate. Martin Doerr (for the SIG) recommended using P130 shows features of, with P130.1 kind of similarity set to "Transcript", to relate the transcription (an E33 Linguistic Object) to the manuscript. João Oliveira had independently suggested the FRBRoo property R58 is derivative of (has derivative) (with R58.1 type = "transcription normalization") as the analogous relation between F1 Works. Martin then explicitly reconciled the two: P130 shows features of is a generalization of R58 is derivative of, so both proposals were correct — P130 being the more general CRM-level property and R58 the more specific FRBRoo Work-level property capturing the same kind of relationship.

question: Did the CIDOC CRM SIG add a way to qualify group membership by role (for example, distinguishing a 'master' from an 'apprentice' within a group) through new sub-properties of group membership, and how was that decided?
gold_answer: Christian-Emil Ore raised the problem that E74 Group could express symmetric relations (e.g. siblings sharing membership of a family) but had no clean way to express asymmetric roles like master/client; Stephen Stead proposed adding role-qualifying sub-properties (P107.1 and P144.1, 'kind of member'), and he and Ore drafted full scope notes and examples ready for a vote. Once circulated, however, Martin reported a negative vote arguing the existing Group/subgroup mechanism (treating each role-holder as a singleton subgroup) already covered the case without any extension, which Ore called 'artificial'. The debate that followed turned on whether membership roles are best seen as 'offices' (a structural feature of the Group itself) or as relational sub-properties, and never reached a stated conclusion on whether to adopt P107.1/P144.1; it drifted instead into a related but separate fix — whether to drop the Group scope note's requirement of 'two or more members' — and the archive in this period records no final decision on the original proposal either way.
key_facts: The trigger was an asymmetric relation (e.g. master/client) that E74 Group's symmetric-membership model could not express directly
Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore drafted P107.1 and P144.1 ('kind of member') qualifiers with full scope notes, intending to bring them to a vote
Martin reported a negative vote proposing singleton subgroups as an alternative to the new properties, which Christian-Emil Ore called 'artificial'
No final decision adopting or rejecting P107.1/P144.1 appears in the discussion; it shifted instead into debating whether to drop the 'two or more members' requirement in the Group scope note
produced_answer: Yes. In Nov 2008 Christian-Emil Ore raised the problem that CRM's Group/membership model (P107 has current or former member) could not express asymmetric roles within a group, such as master vs. apprentice (thread t0426). Stephen Stead proposed solving it with a new 'property of a property' P107.1 (paired with P144.1 on the underlying E85 Joining event) to qualify the kind/role of membership ('in the role of'), as an alternative to modeling master/apprentice as sub-groups or offices. Martin Doerr supported the idea. A formal e-mail vote was called on 2008-11-14 as part of the CRM v4.3->v5.0 change package: 'the addition of properties of properties P107.1, P144.1, as described in the attached proposal' (thread t0427); Stephen Stead and Christian-Emil Ore both voted approve (Stead subject to his text edits). A negative vote then arrived (thread t0431) arguing the master/apprentice case could instead be modeled by treating roles as sub-groups (offices/positions) rather than adding sub-properties, sparking debate about whether roles are relational (favoring P107.1) or structural (favoring sub-groups). Martin Doerr weighed the objection but said he would regard the issue as accepted if no further votes came in. The current ontology entry for P107 (checked via `search.py concept P107`) confirms the sub-property was ultimately adopted and survives in CRM v7.1.3: 'The property P107.1 kind of member can be used to specify the type of membership or the role the member has in the group,' with the worked example 'kind of member husband (E55)'. So the SIG did add the sub-property mechanism, deciding it by a called e-mail vote on the v4.3 change package, over a subsequent (ultimately unsuccessful) objection favoring a sub-group-based alternative.

question: Does the CIDOC CRM provide a direct way to say that one event caused another, and if not, how did the CRM-SIG say causal relationships between events should be handled instead?
gold_answer: No — the SIG declined to add a general 'caused' property between events, arguing that pinning down a single cause is an interpretive, almost judicial act (deciding blame or cause is not the same job as recording facts, likened to the difference between police work and a judge's ruling) and so falls outside what CRM should assert as documented fact. The recommended approach instead is to describe the causing and resulting occurrence as one overlapping process — for example, modelling an event as an E81 Transformation that P123 resulted in the resulting persistent state (an E77 Persistent Item) — or, where a human actor's will is involved, to use P15 influenced/P17 motivated, which is why those properties are restricted to E7 Activities rather than events in general. The position was that CRM should stick to documentable co-occurrence and leave causal interpretation to models built on top of it.
key_facts: CRM-SIG did not add a general 'caused' property between two events
Causation was treated as belonging to interpretation/judgement rather than documentable fact, illustrated by the analogy of police (facts) versus judges (cause/blame)

The recommended workaround is to model cause and effect as a single process, e.g. an E81 Transformation linked via P123 resulted in to the resulting E77 Persistent Item, or to use P15 influenced/P17 motivated when a willing human actor is involved
produced_answer: No — the CRM has no direct 'caused' property between two events/E5 Events. In the October 2011 'Causation and events' thread, Martin Scholz asked how to model that event A caused event B, noting P15_influenced is restricted to E7 Activity (not general E5 Events), P20_had_specific_purpose implies intentional/willful causation only, and P123_resulted_in is restricted to E81 Transformation with an E77 Persistent Item as range — none of them give a general event-to-event 'caused' link, and he proposed inventing a new property. Martin Doerr replied on behalf of the group that this had been discussed repeatedly before and that CRM-SIG deliberately decided NOT to add a causal property: causation is treated as an interpretation/inference concept (comparable to a judge's ruling) that lies outside the CRM's scope of documenting facts. Instead, the CRM-SIG's recommended handling is to describe the concrete facts/processes with existing properties (e.g. treat the cause and effect as one co-occurring process/transformation, using properties like P13_destroyed, P100_was_death_of, P123_resulted_in, or P15_influenced/P17_motivated for activities involving agents) and to let causal inference be left to the data consumer's interpretation rather than asserted directly in the model.

question: When the CIDOC community drafted a recommendation for assigning persistent web identifiers (URIs) to museum objects, what disagreement arose over who should be allowed to mint or aggregate those identifiers, and how did the recommendation's author respond to the objection?
gold_answer: Several reviewers objected that the draft implicitly set up a hierarchy in which one 'best' institution held authority over an object's identifier, when in practice secondary players — art-trade databases, scholarly catalogues, auction indices — often do useful identification work of their own, sometimes ahead of the museum, and competition between identifier-providers can be a healthy part of scholarship rather than a mess to be eliminated. The author held that the recommendation's scope was deliberately narrow — for museums specifically, not for the art trade or scholarship in general — and pointed out it already allowed a delegated 'aggregator' role for a leading community or research index, provided that aggregator publishes a mapping back to the museum's own URI and maintains a documented relationship with the curating institution. He further defended keeping authority concentrated rather than distributed by arguing, from his own published work on co-reference networks, that reconciling identifiers only stays tractable if the network of equivalence links is centered on a small number of focal points rather than spread arbitrarily, since correcting cross-links in an uncontrolled network scales explosively.
key_facts: Reviewers (e.g. Maximilian Schich, Detlev Balzer) objected that the recommendation implied an artificial hierarchy of 'best' identifier authority, when secondary sources like the art trade and scholarly indices often identify objects effectively in practice
The recommendation's author (Martin Doerr) restricted its scope to museums only, not the art trade or research community generally

The recommendation permits a delegated aggregator (a community or research-led index) as long as it publishes a mapping to the museum's own URIs and has a documented relationship with the curating institution

The author argued that identifier reconciliation only remains tractable if kept centered on a small number of focal identifiers in a star-like structure, rather than distributed across many competing peer sources
produced_answer: The recommendation in question was Martin Doerr's/ICOM-CIDOC's 'URIs and Linked Open Data' proposal for museum objects (http://www.cidoc-crm.org/URIs_and_Linked_Open_Data.html), opened for comment on the Crm-sig list in thread t0552 ('Call for Comments', starting 2011-03-21). The main objection, raised first by Maximilian Schich, was to paragraph 10c/11 of the draft, which implied a 'best institution for preserving a particular object's identifier' and let a designated aggregator take a leading role in minting/aggregating URIs for a set of objects. Schich argued this set up 'an artificial hierarchy of authority of who may issue the best identifier,' that in reality there is often no single best-placed institution, and that secondary/non-museum entities (scholars, auction houses like Artprice, online encyclopedias, PhD theses, etc.) should also be encouraged to mint identifiers as a fallback when museums don't, since competition among identifier-producers is part of normal scholarly practice; Vladimir Ivanov agreed with this objection, and Detlev Balzer separately worried that self-appointed 'leading national or community' aggregators would take on prestigious duties they couldn't sustain. Martin Doerr (the recommendation's author) responded on several fronts: he first pushed back that the recommendation's scope was strictly museum objects, not the art trade or cultural objects in general, and asked commenters to stay focused on what was actually proposed. On the substance, he argued that the recommendation already constrains aggregators via conditions in paragraph 11 (an aggregator role only applies if a curating institution takes no action, must never override a curating institution's own URIs, must publish a mapping between its URIs and any URIs the museum later issues, and must have a documented business relationship with the museum) -- and that examples given by objectors as 'good' aggregators (e.g. papyri.info/HGV, kulturarvsdata.se) actually fit and satisfy this leading-role model rather than contradicting it. He also gave a complexity/co-reference argument (citing Meghini, Doerr & Spyratos 2009) that reconciling an unconstrained web of competing identifiers grows exponentially hard, so keeping co-reference clusters star-shaped around a small number of authoritative URIs (ideally the museum's, with a controlled aggregator as fallback) keeps the problem tractable -- 'the more [identifiers], the worse.' He clarified the 'aggregators we fear are those that do not intend to curate their aggregations with scholarly care,' implying the recommendation is not against aggregation per se but against uncurated, uncontrolled minting.

question: The scope notes for the CRM property covering object similarity/derivation, and the parallel property for equivalent alternate names, both described the property as an asymmetric relationship that could nonetheless behave symmetrically in certain cases. A reviewer objected that this was a logical contradiction, since a relation cannot be both symmetric and asymmetric at once. How was this apparent contradiction addressed, and what part of the reviewer's critique was left unresolved?
gold_answer: The response distinguished 'asymmetric' from 'antisymmetric': the property itself is asymmetric, but nothing prevents a narrower subproperty of it from being fully symmetric, and that specialization does not create a logical conflict at the level of the general property — the apparent contradiction came from conflating those two mathematical notions. The word 'dynamic' in the scope notes was clarified to mean that users are expected to create their own subtypes for local semantics, not that a single property instance could be both symmetric and asymmetric simultaneously. However, the reviewer's separate, more concrete objection — that the similarity/derivation property has a defined inverse while the equivalent-appellation property, despite being described in identical terms and being a subproperty of the first, does not — was never addressed, and the reviewer's follow-up proposal to replace the word 'asymmetric' with 'nonsymmetric' throughout also went unanswered.
key_facts: The core contradiction was resolved by distinguishing 'asymmetric' from 'antisymmetric', noting an asymmetric property can have fully symmetric subproperties without logical conflict
'Dynamic' was clarified to mean the property is meant to be subtyped by users for local semantics, not that instances are simultaneously symmetric and asymmetric
The inconsistency that the similarity/derivation property (P130) has a defined inverse while its subproperty for equivalent appellations (P139) does not was left unaddressed
A follow-up proposal to rename 'asymmetric' to 'nonsymmetric' in the scope notes also received no reply
produced_answer: In thread t0554 (Crm-sig, 'Symmetry of P130 and P139', Mar-Apr 2011), Martin Scholz objected that the scope notes of P130 (shows features of/similar to) and P139 (has alternative form) called the properties 'dynamic, asymmetric' while also saying they behave symmetrically when no derivation direction can be established -- which he called a logical contradiction, since a relation cannot be both symmetric and asymmetric (though it can be neither). Martin Doerr (2011-04-01) resolved the apparent contradiction by distinguishing 'asymmetric' from 'antisymmetric': P130 itself is asymmetric (an instance does not imply its inverse holds), but specializations/subproperties of P130 can be defined as symmetric without creating a conflict, since a symmetric subproperty of an asymmetric superproperty is logically fine (he showed the inference chain). He also clarified 'dynamic' meant users are encouraged to create local subtypes, not that the relation itself switches between symmetric and asymmetric. Left unresolved: in his 2011-04-05 follow-up, Scholz noted Doerr's reply did not address the inconsistency that P130 has a defined inverse property while P139 (described identically regarding symmetry, and a subproperty of P130) does not -- he reiterated both should either have inverses or neither should. He also proposed renaming 'asymmetric' to 'nonsymmetric' to avoid the English-language ambiguity between strict mathematical asymmetry and mere absence of symmetry. Neither point received a reply within the thread. A 2021 thread (t1511, 'NEW ISSUE: Scope note of P139') later confirms the P139 side of the fix was still outstanding a decade on, since Doerr notes the asymmetry wording was reformulated for P130 but the corresponding correction was never carried out for P139.

question: Did the CIDOC CRM SIG ever commit to a comprehensive list of disjoint class pairs (classes that can never share a common instance) for the benefit of OWL-style implementations, and if not, what was the reasoning for not doing so?
gold_answer: No — the SIG explicitly and repeatedly declined to produce a comprehensive list of disjoint classes, judging such a list of doubtful practical value and likely to conflict with keeping the standard's class definitions concise. The published guidance confirms only two genuinely fundamental disjoint pairs (Temporal Entity vs. Persistent Item, and Physical Thing vs. Conceptual Object); an earlier effort toward a fuller list was abandoned, with the recommendation on record being to give up on formal disjointness declarations altogether. The stated reasoning was that most other candidate disjoint pairs have real counter-examples in practice — for instance, a single uninterrupted repair act that is simultaneously a removal and an addition of a part, or real linked-data mappings that deliberately model one node as both an Actor and a Collection — so a blanket list would misrepresent how the classes are actually used; the suggested path forward was to evaluate proposed disjoint pairs individually, case by case, with supporting use cases, rather than adopt any general list.
key_facts: Only two disjoint class pairs are confirmed as fundamental in the published guidance: Temporal Entity/Persistent Item and Physical Thing/Conceptual Object
An earlier attempt at a fuller disjointness list was abandoned, with the recorded recommendation being to abandon formal disjoint class declarations altogether

The reasoning given was that most other candidate disjoint pairs have genuine counter-examples in practice (e.g. a single repair event that is both a part removal and a part addition, or real mappings that overload one node as both an Actor and a Collection)
The suggested resolution mechanism was case-by-case evaluation of individually proposed disjoint pairs with use cases, not a comprehensive standing list
produced_answer: No. The CRM-SIG never committed to a comprehensive list of disjoint class pairs. Martin Scholz's 2011-11-22 post to crm-sig ('Implementation recommendation for disjointness', thread t0590) notes that the CIDOC CRM standard explicitly states 'A comprehensive declaration of all possible disjoint class combinations afforded by the CRM has not been provided here; it would be of questionable practical utility, and may easily become inconsistent with the goal of providing a concise definition,' and that issue 92 even proposed to 'abandon the idea of disjoint class declarations altogether.' Martin Doerr's reply in the same thread confirms this was a deliberate decision: 'In the past the CRM-SIG team gave up to define a comprehensive list of disjoint classes, because there were too many exceptions.' He explains only a few pairs are fundamental/unambiguous (E2 Temporal Entity vs E77 Persistent Item; E18 Physical Thing vs E28 Conceptual Object; Time-Span/Place/Dimension), while most other combinations are ambiguous: some classes can legitimately co-apply depending on context (e.g. a Physical Feature treated as synonymous with the Place it occupies), some combine in a genuine ontological sense (e.g. Destruction and Activity), and for events in general it is very hard to assert disjointness because doing so would require excluding any possible interaction between event types and separating their participants/space-time volumes -- he gives the chair-leg mending example (removal + addition documented as two events but possibly one action) to show why. He suggests disjointness statements be handled case-by-case as issues with use cases rather than as a blanket comprehensive list. A 2019-10-08 message from Maria Jose de Almeida (thread t1247, 'Disjointness') shows the same question being asked again years later, indicating no comprehensive list was ever produced in the interim either.
